excerpt: A 2,000 sq ft suite can pay three to four times more per square foot for electrostatic disinfection than a 30,000 sq ft headquarters, almost entirely because of fixed mobilization costs. This guide shows where the price breaks happen and how small and large offices each negotiate the best effective rate.
quickAnswer: Electrostatic disinfection spraying for a 2,000 sq ft office typically costs $0.10 to $0.20 per sq ft per application, often landing on a $90 to $135 per-visit minimum, while 25,000+ sq ft buildings pay $0.03 to $0.08 per sq ft because setup, travel, and documentation are spread across far more area. The biggest price breaks occur around 2,500 sq ft, where minimums stop dominating, and around 10,000 sq ft, where one technician runs a full sprayer shift.

blocks.text: Why Scale Changes Electrostatic Unit Pricing

Every electrostatic disinfection visit carries a fixed cost block before a single surface is sprayed: drive time, unloading the sprayer and charging batteries, mixing disinfectant to label dilution, a walk-through to confirm pre-cleaning, and post-visit documentation with product name, EPA registration number, and dwell time. For most vendors that block runs 45 to 75 minutes of specialty labor billed at $55 to $95 per hour, plus chemical and equipment amortization. On a 2,000 sq ft suite that block is most of the job. On a 40,000 sq ft headquarters it is a rounding error.

Production speed is the variable side. A trained technician with a backpack sprayer covers 8,000 to 15,000 sq ft of open office per hour, versus about 3,500 sq ft per hour for routine ISSA-benchmark janitorial work. Small suites rarely let a technician reach that speed because walls, doors, and private offices interrupt the spray pass. Large open floors let the technician walk long, steady lanes.
Unit Price Breaks by Office Size

blocks.caption: Electrostatic disinfection unit pricing across office sizes (per application, standalone service)

blocks.text: The curve mirrors routine janitorial pricing brackets: $0.12 to $0.20 per sq ft under 2,500 sq ft, $0.09 to $0.15 from 2,500 to 9,999 sq ft, $0.07 to $0.12 from 10,000 to 24,999 sq ft, and $0.05 to $0.10 above 25,000 sq ft. Electrostatic work sits slightly below those numbers at larger sizes because the sprayer is faster than manual cleaning, but slightly above at the smallest sizes because the disinfectant and equipment costs do not shrink.

blocks.title: Two price breaks to know
blocks.text: Around 2,500 sq ft, the per-visit minimum stops controlling the invoice. Around 10,000 sq ft, a single technician can fill a productive two-hour block, and vendors start quoting volume rates. If your office sits just under either threshold, ask whether adjacent common areas can be added to cross it.
Small Suite Strategies: 800 to 5,000 Sq Ft

items: Bundle spraying into the existing janitorial visit so the crew is already on site; this typically removes 15 to 35 percent of the standalone price.
Spray targeted zones only, such as reception, restroom, breakroom, and conference room, and bill per room at $25 to $60 instead of whole-suite square footage.
Share a visit with neighboring tenants in the same building through the property manager, splitting the mobilization block.
Choose lower frequency with better targeting: monthly whole-suite spraying plus weekly manual disinfection of high-touch points often beats weekly spraying on cost.
Ask for a recurring-contract rate; one-time calls nearly always land at the minimum.

blocks.text: Small offices also have more hard-surface square footage per person: reception counters, a single shared breakroom, and one or two restrooms. That makes per-fixture pricing attractive. A small office with two restrooms and one breakroom might pay $60 to $120 per visit for targeted spraying rather than $200 to $400 for whole-suite treatment. Between spraying visits, in-house staff can keep floors clean with a quiet Rubbermaid 421588 executive sweeper in conference rooms and a WaveBrake 35-quart down-press bucket for breakroom mopping, which keeps the pre-cleaning burden low when the sprayer crew arrives.
Large Floor Strategies: 10,000 to 60,000+ Sq Ft

Large offices win on unit price but lose on total budget, so the negotiation shifts from rate to scope. A 40,000 sq ft headquarters spraying weekly at $0.045 per sq ft pays $1,800 per application, or $7,794 per month at 4.33 visits. Dropping to targeted weekly spraying of 12,000 sq ft of high-touch zones, plus monthly whole-floor treatment, cuts that to about $3,300 per month without reducing coverage where people actually touch surfaces.

items.name: Zone the floor plate
items.text: Separate open workstations, conference rooms, restrooms, breakrooms, lobbies, and fitness rooms on a floor plan with square footage for each zone.

items.name: Assign frequency by zone
items.text: Spray restrooms, breakrooms, and elevator lobbies more often than private offices or low-use storage.

items.name: Ask for tiered pricing
items.text: Request separate rates for weekly zones and monthly full-floor passes so you are not paying whole-floor rates for partial work.

items.name: Require crew sizing disclosure
items.text: Confirm technicians per shift and hours per visit; a 40,000 sq ft floor should not take more than five to six technician-hours.

items.name: Benchmark annually
items.text: Rebid or renegotiate yearly with your actual service logs as evidence of production rates.

blocks.title: Large-site compliance load
blocks.text: Bigger buildings bring more OSHA HazCom obligations: Safety Data Sheets posted for every disinfectant used, labeled secondary containers, and documented training for any in-house staff who handle the product. Ask the vendor to provide re-entry interval signage for each zone so occupants do not return before the label dwell time is complete.

Consider two clients of the same vendor. A 2,000 sq ft accounting firm sprays monthly at $0.14 per sq ft, paying $280 per visit and $3,360 per year. A 30,000 sq ft software company sprays biweekly at $0.05 per sq ft, paying $1,500 per visit at 2.17 visits per month, or about $39,060 per year. The software company pays 11.6 times more in total but only about 36 percent as much per sq ft per application. Both are fairly priced; the difference is scale, not vendor margin.

faqs.q: Why does my 1,500 sq ft office pay more per square foot than a large building?
faqs.a: Fixed costs such as travel, setup, chemical mixing, and documentation consume most of a small visit. Those costs are the same whether the vendor sprays 1,500 or 15,000 sq ft, so the per-sq-ft rate for small suites is often two to four times higher.

faqs.q: At what size do volume discounts start?
faqs.a: Most vendors move off minimum pricing around 2,500 sq ft and begin offering volume rates near 10,000 sq ft, where one technician fills a productive block. Additional breaks often appear at 25,000 sq ft, matching standard janitorial size brackets.

faqs.q: Can small offices avoid the minimum charge?
faqs.a: Yes, by bundling spraying into a scheduled janitorial visit, using per-room pricing for only high-touch areas, or coordinating with neighboring tenants through the property manager so one mobilization covers several suites.

faqs.q: Should large offices spray the entire floor every visit?
faqs.a: Usually not. Zoning lets you spray high-touch areas like restrooms, breakrooms, and lobbies weekly and treat the full floor monthly, which can cut spraying spend by 40 percent or more while keeping coverage where it matters.

faqs.q: Does the vendor need different insurance for large sites?
faqs.a: Many property managers require higher limits for large buildings, commonly $2 million general liability aggregate plus umbrella coverage, with the owner and manager named as additional insured on the COI. Confirm requirements in your lease or building rules before awarding the contract.
